name: Benedict of Nursia
knownFor: Founder of the monasteries of Subiaco and Monte Cassino and author of the Rule for monks, whose life is known through Gregory the Great's Dialogues; the Frankish church took up his Rule to restore the monastic life, and in 802 Charlemagne ordered monasteries put right by it.
dates: Born, by Edmund Gardner, about 480, and by Francis Gasquet in 480; died, by the tradition of his order, in 543, as both give it. Gregory the Great gives no years. Gardner dates the founding of Monte Cassino to 528 or 529
role: Monk and abbot; author of the Rule

keyWorks.title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
keyWorks.about: a prologue and seventy-three chapters on the life of a monastery: obedience, the hours of prayer, manual work and holy reading, the abbot, and the reception of guests as Christ; at its end it calls itself a little rule for beginners

traces: His Rule, which Gregory the Great calls "excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style", survives in Latin, and Francis Gasquet and Oswald Hunter Blair translate it into English.
Gregory says he built twelve monasteries near Subiaco, with twelve monks in each, before he founded Monte Cassino.

Carloman, duke of the Franks, had his council of 742 tell monks and nuns to live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, and at the next council the abbots and monks received it "ad restaurandam normam regularis vitae".
In 802, the annals of Lorsch say, Charlemagne had the abbots and monks at Aachen read the Rule together and ordered whatever in the monasteries went against it to be put right by it.
remembered: Gregory the Great gave the whole second book of his Dialogues to his miracles and wrote that "the holy man could not otherwise teach, than himself lived."

Gregory names the four disciples he had his stories from: Constantinus, the next abbot after him; Valentinianus, long in charge of the Lateran monastery; Simplicius, the third head of his order; and Honoratus, abbot of the house where Benedict first began.

uncertain: Nearly all that is known of his life comes from one witness, Gregory the Great's Dialogues, a book of miracles written to honor a saint. Gregory says he could not learn all that Benedict did and had his stories from four disciples. At least one story he had at second hand: Honoratus heard it from other monks.

Gregory gives no years. The birth about 480 and the death in 543 are Edmund Gardner's and Francis Gasquet's; both call 543 the tradition. Gardner says the date he left Rome is disputed and puts it a few years before 500.
Gasquet thinks Benedict probably conceived the Rule at Subiaco and finished it at Monte Cassino. Gregory says only that he wrote it.

The Rule points its readers to older guides: "the Collations of the Fathers, their Institutes, their Lives, and the Rule of our Holy Father St. Basil." Gardner says it was based in part on Basil's rule.

What the Rule did. Francis Gasquet, a Benedictine editor, judges that the Rule put a written code in place of an abbot's personal will, and calls it practically the only monastic Rule of the West from the ninth to the twelfth century.
The second council. The edition of the capitularies records that Hefele and Hahn held the council of Estinnes to be Carloman's and Pippin's together; its editor argues it was Carloman's.

The modern English of Benedict's words to Totila, "You do many evil things", follows Gregory's Latin, "Multa mala facis, multa mala fecisti" (Acta Sanctorum, March, vol. 3), which has no word for "daily"; the 1608 English adds it. "Outstanding for its sound judgment and clear in its language" likewise leaves out the 1608 "also", which the Latin lacks.

briefReferences: Dialogues II, prologue, tr. 1608, ed. Edmund G. Gardner: born in the province of Nursia, sent to Rome to study, students falling into loose living; his four disciples as Gregory's sources. Book II is the only early Life of Benedict, and Gregory tells it to show the miracles of a holy man.
Dialogues II.1: Subiaco, almost forty miles from Rome; Romanus, the cave for three years, the bread on a rope with a little bell; others coming to him for teaching.
Dialogues II.3: the nearby monastery that made him abbot, the poisoned wine and the shattered glass; the twelve monasteries near Subiaco.
Dialogues II.8: the move to Cassino. Gardner: about 528 or 529.
Dialogues II.14: "in the time of the Goths".
Rule, Prologue (Latin, ed. Oswald Hunter Blair; English, tr. Francis Aidan Gasquet): a school for the Lord's service, nothing harsh, nothing heavy.
Rule, ch. 48: "Idleness is an enemy of the soul"; set times for manual labor and holy reading. Ch. 64: the abbot chosen by the community, who tempers all things.
Dialogues II.17: the Lombards plunder Monte Cassino by night, and no monk is taken.
Paul the Deacon, History of the Langobards IV.17, tr. Foulke: the monks flee to Rome with the manuscript of the Rule.
MGH Capitularia I, no. 10: Carloman, duke of the Franks, and his council of 742; the Rule for monks and nuns in the lands he ruled.
MGH Capitularia I, the Aachen synod of 802, from the annals of Lorsch: the Rule read, and the monasteries put right by it.
World census, Early Benedictine / Italian Monasticism: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: So we must found a school for the Lord's service. In founding it, we hope to lay down nothing harsh and nothing heavy.
quotationOriginals.printed: We are therefore now about to institute a school for the service of God, in which we hope nothing harsh nor burdensome will be ordained.
quotationOriginals.original: Constituenda est ergo nobis Dominici schola servitii; in qua institutione nihil asperum, nihil grave nos constituturos speramus.
quotationOriginals.work: Benedict, Rule, Prologue; Latin ed. Oswald Hunter Blair, English tr. Francis Aidan Gasquet
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from the Latin. "in qua institutione" is read as the founding, and "Dominici" as "the Lord's"; Gasquet reads "in which" as the school and says "God". The OCR reads "servitu" for "servitii"; line 1242 holds only marginal dates.

quotationOriginals.modern: Let him so temper everything that the strong have something to long for, and the weak do not run away.
quotationOriginals.printed: let him so temper all things that the strong may have their scope and the weak be not scared.
quotationOriginals.original: sic omnia temperet, ut et sit quod fortes cupiant, et infirmi non refugiant
quotationOriginals.work: Benedict, Rule, ch. 64, of the abbot; Latin ed. Oswald Hunter Blair, English tr. Francis Aidan Gasquet
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from the Latin. "refugiant" is read as the weak fleeing of themselves; Gasquet's "be not scared" is looser.
